manuscript_meta.title: SPARSELY-CONNECTED NEURAL NETWORKS: TO- WARDS EFFICIENT VLSI IMPLEMENTATION OF DEEP NEURAL NETWORKS

report.summary: This manuscript introduces 'sparsely-connected networks' as a method to improve the efficiency of deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly targeting the high parameter count in fully-connected layers. The core idea is to randomly remove connections using masks generated by Linear-Feedback Shift Registers (LFSRs), a hardware-friendly technique. The authors demonstrate through experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, and SVHN that this approach can reduce connections by up to 90% while, in many cases, improving classification accuracy compared to dense counterparts. A key contribution is the proposal of a corresponding VLSI architecture that leverages this sparsity to achieve significant savings in memory area (up to 90%) and energy consumption (up to 84%) for a single neuron.

points: The paper addresses a critical and highly relevant problem: the high computational and memory cost of DNNs, which is a major barrier to their deployment on resource-constrained hardware.

The proposed solution is not purely algorithmic; it is designed with hardware implementation in mind from the start, culminating in a concrete VLSI architecture proposal. This link between algorithm and hardware is a significant strength.
The use of LFSRs to generate connection masks is a simple yet effective method that avoids the overhead of storing explicit sparsity maps, which is a common issue in other pruning techniques.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive, testing the method across three standard datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10, SVHN) and comparing it not only to standard dense networks but also to other hardware-focused techniques like BinaryConnect and TernaryConnect.
The results are compelling, showing that significant sparsity can be introduced not just without performance loss, but often with an accuracy improvement, suggesting a regularizing effect.

The manuscript contains a critical citation error. Reference [34] is fabricated, linking to a completely different paper than the one listed. This represents a serious breach of academic standards and severely undermines the credibility of the work.

The bibliography suffers from widespread formatting and referencing issues. 28 of the 39 citations could not be automatically resolved, indicating missing DOIs, incorrect metadata, or inconsistent formatting. This makes it difficult for readers to trace the cited work.

The VLSI implementation results, while impressive, are reported for a single neuron. This analysis does not account for system-level effects, such as memory bank conflicts, interconnect overhead, or control logic for an entire layer, which could diminish the projected savings.

The paper fails to cite or discuss a highly-cited seminal work directly relevant to efficient network design ('Seven Defining Features of Terahertz (THz) Wireless Systems, 2022'). This omission weakens the paper's positioning within the current literature and calls into question the thoroughness of the background research.

detailed_comments.comment: A critical issue exists in the bibliography. Reference [34] is listed as 'Stochastic computing can improve upon digital spiking neural networks' (2016), but the provided DOI (10.1109/cvpr.2015.7298594) corresponds to a completely different paper, 'Going deeper with convolutions' (2015). This is a major, fabricated reference that must be addressed immediately. Furthermore, 28 of the 39 references could not be programmatically verified, indicating systemic issues with formatting or missing identifiers. The authors are strongly urged to conduct a thorough audit of their entire reference list to correct all errors and ensure every citation is accurate, complete, and correctly linked.

The reported energy and area savings of 84% and 90% respectively are very promising. However, these figures are for a single neuron. To make a more compelling case for the practical impact of the proposed architecture, it would be beneficial to provide an analysis or at least a well-reasoned projection of the savings at the level of a full sparsely-connected layer. This would involve considering the overhead of instantiating multiple neuron units and the shared memory access controller.

The paper convincingly shows that sparsity can improve accuracy. The text suggests this is due to a regularization effect, which is plausible. It would strengthen the paper to elaborate on this point. For instance, does the random, unstructured nature of the sparsity play a key role? A brief comparison or discussion against structured pruning methods at similar sparsity levels could provide valuable context and further support the claims about the benefits of this specific approach.

The footnotes in Tables 2, 3, and 4, which clarify that binarized/ternarized algorithms were used for training but single-precision weights were used for testing, are crucial for interpreting the results. This detail is somewhat buried. Please consider highlighting this methodological point more prominently in the main body of Section 4 to avoid any potential misinterpretation by the reader.

questions: Can you please clarify the discrepancy for reference [34]? Was this an error in compiling the bibliography, and what is the correct citation for the claim it was intended to support? This is a critical issue of academic integrity.

The VLSI analysis focuses on a single neuron. How do you anticipate the reported energy and area savings will scale when implementing a full layer with hundreds or thousands of neurons, including the necessary control logic and memory organization?

The paper notes that the proposed network acts as a regularizer. Have you performed any experiments to compare the regularization effect of your LFSR-based random sparsity against other regularization techniques like Dropout at an equivalent rate?
report.overall_assessment: This paper presents a valuable and timely contribution to the field of efficient deep learning. The core idea of using LFSR-generated masks for creating sparsely-connected networks is elegant, practical, and well-supported by strong empirical results across multiple datasets. The inclusion of a VLSI architecture and synthesis results is a commendable step that grounds the work in real-world application. However, the manuscript is critically flawed by a severe issue of scholarly integrity: the presence of what appears to be a fabricated reference. This, combined with numerous other citation inaccuracies and the failure to cite relevant seminal work, makes the paper unacceptable for publication in its current form. While the technical core of the work is strong, it cannot be properly evaluated or trusted until these fundamental scholarly issues are fully resolved.

reviewer_council.summary: This manuscript introduces 'sparsely-connected networks' as a method to improve the efficiency of deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly targeting the high parameter count in fully-connected layers. The core idea is to randomly remove connections using masks generated by Linear-Feedback Shift Registers (LFSRs), a hardware-friendly technique. The authors demonstrate through experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, and SVHN that this approach can reduce connections by up to 90% while, in many cases, improving classification accuracy compared to dense counterparts. A key contribution is the proposal of a corresponding VLSI architecture that leverages this sparsity to achieve significant savings in memory area (up to 90%) and energy consumption (up to 84%) for a single neuron.

findings.title: Sparsely-Connected Ağlar ve Donanım Mimarisi ile Önemli Katkı
findings.summary: Makale, derin öğrenme modellerinin donanım uygulamalarındaki bellek ve güç tüketimi sorunlarına yönelik, seyreltik bağlantılı sinir ağları ve bunlara özel verimli bir VLSI mimarisi önererek önemli bir özgün katkı sunmaktadır.

manuscript_anchors.quote: In this paper, we propose sparsely-connected networks, by showing that the number of connections in fully-connected networks can be reduced by up to 90% while improving the accuracy performance on three popular datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10 and SVHN). We then propose an efﬁcient hardware architecture based on linear-feedback shift registers to reduce the memory requirements of the proposed sparsely-connected networks. The proposed architecture can save up to 90% of memory compared to the conventional implementations of fully-connected neural networks. Moreover, imple- mentation results show up to 84% reduction in the energy consumption of a single neuron of the proposed sparsely-connected networks compared to a single neuron of fully-connected neural networks.

In this paper, we propose sparsely-connected networks by randomly removing some of the con- nections in fully-connected networks. Random connection masks are generated by linear-feedback shift registers (LFSRs), which are also used in the VLSI implementation to disable the connec- tions. Experimental results on three commonly used datasets show that the proposed networks can improve network accuracy while removing up to 90% of the connections. Additionally, we apply the proposed algorithm on top of the binarizing/ternarizing technique achieving a better misclassiﬁca- tion rate than the best binarized/ternarized networks reported in literature.
